info.bio: Sly Stone (born Sylvester Stewart, 15 March 1943, in Denton, Texas; died 9 June, 2025) was an American musician, songwriter, and record producer, most famous for his role as frontman for Sly & the Family Stone, a band which played a critical role in the development of soul, funk and psychedelia in the 1960s and 1970s. Sly & the Family Stone was started in Vallejo, California and eventually had artists from around the San Francisco Bay Area.

scenes.name: San Francisco: Acid Tests y Haight-Ashbury
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: A principios de 1966 había distritos psicodélicos con locales, grupos, ropa, impresos y drogas propios en Londres, Los Ángeles y San Francisco. Los Merry Pranksters de Ken Kesey convirtieron su desafío «Can You Pass the Acid Test?» en fiestas de luces, cine y sonido grabado y devuelto al instante: la segunda, en San José en diciembre de 1965 tras un concierto de los Stones, y nueve más en los tres primeros meses de 1966 (cinco en Los Ángeles, una en Watts). Los beats se habían mudado de North Beach a Haight-Ashbury; los Thelin abrieron la Psychedelic Shop y con Stewart Brand se hizo el Trips Festival (6.000 personas). La banda sonora era Rubber Soul. El caos sustituía al cuidado de Leary por el «set and setting»: en el Acid Test de Watts, Ken Babbs amplificó por micrófono los gritos de una chica en pleno mal viaje.

scenes.name: The Funk: un movimiento musical y social
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Para George Clinton, el funk es algo que se siente y que todo el mundo puede sentir, pero cuanto más se piensa más cuesta pillarlo; despojada hasta la raíz, toda la música negra es funk, «el producto que producimos, y nadie lo hace como nosotros». Rickey Vincent, locutor del programa The History of Funk en la radio universitaria KALX de Berkeley (The Uhuru Maggot), escribe para quien reconoce en un rap un riff o un grito sacado de un tema funk de los setenta, y para quienes crecieron con James Brown, P-Funk, Sly, Kool & the Gang, Earth, Wind & Fire y los Ohio Players sin que nadie les reconociera un lugar en la historia como movimiento musical y social. El funk pasó décadas en la sombra, tratado como un derivado del soul, ridiculizado y hasta temido, mientras el disco se inventaba para llevar sus elementos calientes a las masas en forma esterilizada; hoy está en sintonías, programas nocturnos y en el hip hop, su ahijado. Vincent plantea que entre los disturbios de Newark (1967) y el caso Bakke (1977) hubo otro renacimiento cultural negro, como el de Harlem tras Garvey, y que su sonido fue The Funk. El libro nació de su tesis «Funk as a Paradigm of Black Consciousness».

scenes.name: Contracultura, Sgt. Pepper y Woodstock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La revolución negra sacudió también a la juventud blanca: la cuestión moral de los derechos civiles, el racismo familiar, la atracción por la cultura negra, el miedo al reclutamiento y las drogas. Dylan y los Beatles convirtieron el rock en forma de vida. Sgt. Pepper (1967), de unos Beatles criados con Chuck Berry («a mí no me ha pasado nada desde 1958, cuando oí el rock and roll negro», dijo Lennon), abrió la era psicodélica que influiría en Electric Ladyland de Hendrix y en el Free Your Mind… de Funkadelic; Sly salió en el Ed Sullivan con uniforme de banda, y de ahí viene el púrpura de Prince. La contracultura sintetizó jazz, R&B, pop, rock y folk en formas largas, espectáculos de luces y tecnología, rasgos que el black rock (Hendrix, Sly, Funkadelic, War, Ohio Players, los Isley, Bar-Kays) llevó al funk. En Woodstock (1969) brillaron Hendrix, Sly y Santana. Las muertes de Hendrix, Joplin y Morrison, Altamont, Kent State y Jackson State acabaron con la idea de que el rock cambiaría el mundo; en la música negra el funk mantuvo vivos esos ideales.

scenes.name: Sly and the Family Stone
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El embajador del funk ante la América blanca. Sylvester Stewart, DJ de KSOL y productor de Autumn Records, reunió una banda mixta de hombres y mujeres, negros y blancos, todos músicos y cantantes: su hermano Freddie a la guitarra, Larry Graham al bajo, Cynthia Robinson a la trompeta, Jerry Martini al saxo, Greg Errico a la batería y su hermana Rose. Fue la primera banda autosuficiente y polivalente, sin barreras raciales ni de género, y el primer rockero negro empaquetado por la industria (CBS): podía tocar en el Apollo o en el Fillmore y era ideal para la televisión en color. «Dance to the Music» (1968) unió a las discotecas del mundo; Stand! (1969) creó el formato del disco funk, con baile, rock, una sesión de sexo de trece minutos, pop e himnos de orgullo negro; en Woodstock fue lo mejor del festival. «Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)» (1970) abrió la década del funk. Luego se encerró: There’s a Riot Going On (1971), oscuro, turbio y hecho casi solo, desconcertó a los críticos blancos pero es una obra maestra del funk; Fresh (1973) fue aún mejor. Después vinieron la retirada, giras con Clinton y una detención por cocaína en 1981. Sus imitadores ligeros (Jackson 5, Commodores) y los grandes espectáculos de Earth, Wind & Fire, P-Funk, Michael Jackson y Prince salen de él: «el Padrino abrió la puerta, pero Sly dejó entrar a todo el mundo».

podcast.title: Sly Stone Death (2025) – COPD After Living in a Van and $5M Settlement
podcast.body: Sly Stone, pioneer of funk, soul, and rock, died in 2025 of COPD. After years of personal struggles that included living in a camper van, he won a $5 million copyright lawsuit that allowed a brief return to public life before his death. "After years of struggles and living in a camper van, won a $5 million copyright lawsuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Burden of African American Stardom
podcast.body: The immense expectations placed on Sly Stone, not only as a superstar but specifically as an African American superstar, were perceived to be a significant burden on him. Questlove's documentary explores this aspect in greater depth. "ultimately the expectations on Sly to be not just a superstar but an African American one I think proved to be too much of a burden."

podcast.title: Clyde Davis's Influence
podcast.body: Following the commercial failure of Sly and the Family Stone's first album, "A Whole New Thing," Sly Stone was encouraged by CBS Records executive Clyde Davis to write music more suited for radio. This directive led to the creation of songs like "Dance to the Music." "after that Sly wrote more for the radio because well that's what CBS records executive Clyde Davis told him to do giving us dance to the music."

podcast.title: Death and Legacy
podcast.body: Sly Stone passed away on Monday, June 9th, 2025, at the age of 82, a lifespan many considered longer than expected given his personal struggles. His notorious drug use, subsequent erratic behavior, and frequent missed shows are cited as reasons why he has not been collectively remembered as the musical genius he clearly was. "No doubt 82 was longer than many people ever expected him to live."

podcast.title: Influence on Bee Gees' Bass Sound
podcast.body: Sly Stone's bass sound was openly emulated by the Bee Gees on their 1975 number one single "Jive Talkin'," indicating his foundational impact on popular music. "the Bee Gees were openly emulating the bass sound of Stevie Wonder and Sly Stone."

podcast.title: Innovator of 1960s Funk
podcast.body: Sly Stone is recognized as a key innovator of funk in the 1960s, whose contributions were taken up by a rising generation of syncopated bands and soulful singers in the first half of the 1970s. "the 60s innovations of... Sly Stone... were taken up by a rising generation of syncopated bands and soulful singers."

podcast.body: In 2023, Sly Stone published his memoir titled "Thank You for Letting Me Be Myself Again." This publication marked a return to the public eye after a period of musical inactivity. "You can go read his 2023 memoir. Thank you for letting me be myself again."

podcast.title: Musical Inactivity Period
podcast.body: Sly Stone effectively dropped off the musical radar in 1982, remaining largely inactive until the publication of his memoir and Questlove's documentary brought renewed attention to his work. "When musically he dropped off the radar in 1982 that was really kind of it until he was he published his memoir and then Quest Love did the documentary."

podcast.title: Questlove's Documentary
podcast.body: A documentary about Sly Stone, titled "Sly Lives," directed by Questlove, began streaming on Hulu approximately six months prior to Stone's death. This film delves into the "demons" and personal burdens faced by Sly Stone, including the significant pressure of being not just a superstar, but an African American one. "You could go watch Quest Love's documentary on Sly Sly Lives, which began streaming on Hulu about six months ago."

podcast.title: Template for 70s Music
podcast.body: Sly Stone is recognized for providing a foundational template for the music of the 1970s, particularly through his innovative use of instrumentation and sound. His work showed what was musically possible and influenced subsequent acts. "another example of how Sly gave us a template for 70s music."

xref.title: Esteemed Fans and Original Songwriting
xref.body: Before their breakup in 1975, Fanny garnered a significant following that included David Bowie, John Lennon, George Harrison, and Sly Stone. They released five major label albums and notably wrote all their own songs, a rare feat for female artists at the time. "David Bowie, John and George from The Beatles, Slice Stone, and a ton of other big names became huge fans. They released five major label albums and they wrote all their own songs, which is something almost no female artists did back in those days."
